body:
Nationalism and communal politics

The Indian national movement developed through the struggle against British colonial rule. It sought political freedom and the right of Indians to govern themselves. However, political organisations differed over how India's religious, social and regional communities should be represented in a future government.

The Indian National Congress generally sought to build a national movement representing Indians across religious communities. Other organisations increasingly argued that particular religious communities required separate political safeguards. Disagreements over representation, combined with competition for political power and episodes of communal violence, became important factors in the events leading to Partition in 1947.

Communalism

In modern Indian history, communalism refers to a form of politics that treats religious communities as separate political groups with potentially conflicting interests and seeks to mobilise people primarily through those identities. It can become especially divisive when one religious community is presented as naturally opposed to another.

Religious identity and communal politics are not identical. A person may practise a religion without believing that members of different religions must have opposing political interests. Similarly, members of the same religion may disagree over class, region, language, political ideology and constitutional arrangements.

The Indian National Congress

The Indian National Congress was established in December 1885 at Bombay, where 72 delegates attended its first session. Its early leadership included W.C. Bonnerjee, Dadabhai Naoroji, Badruddin Tyabji and other prominent public figures. A.O. Hume, a retired British official, helped bring political leaders from different regions together.

The early Congress demanded greater Indian participation in administration, representative legislative councils, civil service opportunities and economic reforms. Its leadership was initially concentrated among educated professionals, but it claimed to speak for Indians across communities.

During the early 20th century, the Congress increasingly adopted mass political methods such as boycott, public demonstrations, non-cooperation and civil disobedience. These campaigns attempted to bring people from different religious and social backgrounds into a common struggle against colonial rule.

The 1905 Partition of Bengal

In 1905, Viceroy Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal. The British administration presented the measure as an administrative reform. Indian nationalists, however, regarded it as an attempt to weaken Bengali political influence and divide the population.

The decision produced the Swadeshi Movement, which encouraged the boycott of British goods, the use of Indian products, national education and public mobilisation. Although both moderate and radical nationalists opposed Bengal's partition, political responses were not uniform across communities.

The 1905 division of Bengal must be distinguished from the 1947 Partition of British India. The first was a colonial reorganisation of a province; the second created 2 independent Dominions and divided Punjab and Bengal.

Formation of the All-India Muslim League

The All-India Muslim League was founded at Dacca, now Dhaka, in December 1906. Its early leadership included Muslim landlords, nawabs and educated political figures who wanted safeguards for Muslim political interests.

The League initially sought to protect Muslim interests within British India. It did not begin in 1906 with a demand for the separate sovereign state that eventually emerged in 1947.

The League's early politics placed particular emphasis on adequate representation in legislative institutions. The British decision to introduce separate electorates for Muslims in 1909 strengthened the importance of religion-based political representation.

The Hindu Mahasabha, founded in 1915, was another organisation that sought to mobilise political support around religious identity. It attempted to promote Hindu political unity across caste and sectarian divisions. Neither the League nor the Mahasabha represented every member of the religious community in whose name it spoke.

Prelims focus

  • 1885: Indian National Congress established at Bombay.
  • 1905: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal; the Swadeshi Movement opposed the decision.
  • 1906: All-India Muslim League founded at Dacca.
  • 1909: Separate electorates introduced for Muslims.
  • 1915: Hindu Mahasabha established.
  • Trap: The Muslim League's establishment in 1906 did not mean that the Pakistan demand already existed in its final form.

[NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 110–114; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Understanding Partition, printed pp. 382–385; UK Parliament, Hansard, Indian Councils Bill, 1 April 1909, consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Indian Nationalism and the Emergence of Communal Politics

body:
Meaning of separate electorates

A separate electorate is an electoral arrangement in which voters belonging to a designated community elect representatives from that community through a separate electoral process.

Under the separate electorates introduced for Muslims in British India, Muslim voters on the relevant electoral register elected representatives for designated Muslim seats. Voters belonging to other communities did not elect those representatives.

The arrangement was intended to provide political safeguards for Muslim representation. However, it also encouraged politicians to organise political support through separate religious constituencies.

Separate electorate and reserved seat

Separate electorate: A designated community elects its representatives through a separate body of voters.

Reserved seat with a joint electorate: A seat is reserved for candidates belonging to a specified community or category, but eligible voters in the common constituency participate in electing its representative.

The distinction concerns who votes, not merely who is eligible to contest the seat. A reserved seat does not automatically imply a separate electorate.

The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909

The Indian Councils Act, 1909, commonly called the Morley-Minto Reforms, introduced separate electorates for Muslims in the legislative councils.

The reforms are associated with John Morley, the Secretary of State for India, and Lord Minto, the Viceroy of India.

The Act expanded legislative councils and introduced electoral arrangements that provided separate Muslim representation. It did not establish universal adult suffrage or responsible government based on a freely elected Indian legislature. Voting rights remained limited by the electoral qualifications then in force.

The constitutional importance of the reform lay in the official recognition of religious community as a basis for electoral representation. This became an important issue in later Congress-League negotiations.

The Lucknow Pact of December 1916

The Lucknow Pact was a political agreement between the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League in December 1916.

The 2 organisations agreed on a common constitutional reform programme and supported the demand for greater representative government in India.

An important provision was the Congress acceptance of separate electorates for Muslims, together with agreed arrangements for Muslim representation in legislative councils.

This acceptance represented a political compromise. Congress leaders hoped that cooperation with the League would strengthen the movement for constitutional reform, while the League obtained recognition of the safeguards it considered necessary.

The pact should be understood alongside the reunion of the moderate and extremist sections of the Congress during this period. It provided a broader political platform for nationalist demands.

What the Lucknow Pact did not do

The Lucknow Pact did not introduce separate electorates for the first time. The British had already introduced them in 1909. The pact represented the Congress acceptance of the principle as part of a negotiated constitutional arrangement in 1916.

The later distinction illustrated by the Poona Pact

A different dispute over representation arose in 1932, when the British Communal Award provided for separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar supported separate political safeguards for the Depressed Classes because he considered independent political representation important for overcoming social discrimination.

Mahatma Gandhi opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, fearing that they would further divide Hindu society. He began a fast against the arrangement.

The resulting Poona Pact of September 1932 provided reserved legislative seats for the Depressed Classes within joint electorates, rather than separate electorates for that category.

This agreement did not abolish the separate Muslim electorates established under earlier constitutional arrangements. The Poona Pact is therefore an important example of why reservation of seats and separation of electorates must not be confused.

Why the distinction mattered

Political organisations disagreed about whether minorities would receive adequate representation in a common electoral system. Supporters of separate electorates argued that these arrangements protected communities from domination by a numerical majority. Critics feared that they would deepen religious divisions by making community identity a permanent basis of electoral competition.

The disagreement concerned constitutional safeguards and political power. A demand for separate electorates did not, by itself, amount to a demand for a separate sovereign country.

Prelims focus

  • Indian Councils Act, 1909: Introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
  • Morley and Minto: Secretary of State for India and Viceroy respectively.
  • Lucknow Pact, December 1916: Agreement between Congress and Muslim League.
  • Poona Pact, September 1932: Reserved seats for Depressed Classes under joint electorates.
  • Trap: Separate electorate and reserved seat are not interchangeable terms.

[NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 114–115; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World II, Class 10, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 68–69; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Understanding Partition, printed p. 383; UK Parliament, Hansard, Indian Councils Bill, 1 April 1909, and East India Revenue Accounts, 5 August 1909, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Separate electorates and joint electorates differ in who chooses the representative.

title: Separate Electorates, Reserved Seats and the Lucknow Pact of 1916

body:
From elite politics to mass participation

The national movement changed significantly after the First World War. Political activity increasingly involved peasants, workers, students, traders, women and other sections of society rather than remaining concentrated among educated political leaders.

The war had increased taxation, prices and economic hardship. Repressive colonial legislation and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919 intensified opposition to British rule.

Mahatma Gandhi attempted to unite different communities through satyagraha, or active non-violent resistance based on truth and the willingness to suffer rather than inflict violence on opponents.

The Khilafat Movement

The Khilafat Movement developed after the First World War because many Indian Muslims opposed the proposed treatment of the Ottoman Sultan, who was also regarded as the Khalifa.

The movement sought protection for the Khalifa's position and authority, including his connection with important Muslim sacred places.

The principal Indian Khilafat leaders included Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, commonly known as the Ali brothers.

Gandhi supported the Khilafat cause because he believed that cooperation between Hindu and Muslim political movements could strengthen the wider struggle against British rule.

A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919. During 1920, Gandhi and the Ali brothers mobilised support for collective action.

The Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement

At the special Congress session in Calcutta in September 1920, Gandhi secured support for launching non-cooperation in connection with the Khilafat issue and the demand for swaraj.

The Congress adopted the Non-Cooperation programme at its Nagpur session in December 1920. The movement began in January 1921.

Its principal methods included:

  • Boycotting government-controlled educational institutions.
  • Surrendering British titles and honours.
  • Boycotting legislative councils and foreign goods.
  • Picketing liquor shops and promoting Indian-made goods.
  • Encouraging people to withdraw voluntary cooperation from colonial institutions.

Congress leaders sought political independence, while Khilafat leaders also pursued specific concerns relating to the Ottoman Caliphate. Their cooperation demonstrated that organisations with different immediate objectives could participate in a common anti-colonial campaign.

However, participation varied across regions and communities. A common nationalist programme did not eliminate differences in political priorities.

Violence and the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation

Gandhi insisted that satyagraha should remain non-violent. On 4 February 1922, a crowd attacked and burned a police station at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district. Following the incident, Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922.

The incident demonstrated the difficulty of maintaining non-violent discipline in a large mass movement.

Distinguish 2 kinds of violence

Revolutionary or anti-colonial violence was directed against colonial authority or its institutions as part of a struggle for political change. Communal violence involved attacks on people or communities identified primarily by religion. The motivations and targets were different, even though both involved violence.

Civil Disobedience and Gujarat's role

After the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation, the national movement continued through other political methods. Congress adopted the demand for Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, at its Lahore session in December 1929.

In 1930, Gandhi launched the Salt Satyagraha from Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The march began on 12 March 1930 and reached Dandi on the Gujarat coast. On 6 April 1930, Gandhi broke the colonial salt law.

The Salt Satyagraha became a central part of the Civil Disobedience Movement. Unlike ordinary non-cooperation, civil disobedience involved deliberately breaking unjust colonial laws through organised protest.

Women, peasants, traders and other groups participated. The Patidar peasants of Gujarat were among the important rural participants in the Civil Disobedience Movement, particularly because of grievances concerning land revenue during economic hardship.

Mass mobilisation and communal divisions

Mass nationalist movements created opportunities for cooperation across religions. Nevertheless, political unity remained uneven. Some Muslim organisations and leaders became increasingly distant from Congress after the decline of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation campaigns.

Religious processions, competing political claims and communal clashes during the 1920s and 1930s contributed to mutual distrust. The growth of national mass politics therefore occurred alongside the growth of communal political competition.

Prelims focus

  • 1919: Khilafat Committee formed in Bombay; Ali brothers were major leaders.
  • December 1920: Congress adopted the Non-Cooperation programme at Nagpur.
  • January 1921: Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement began.
  • February 1922: Gandhi withdrew Non-Cooperation following Chauri Chaura.
  • 6 April 1930: Salt law broken at Dandi, Gujarat.
  • Trap: The Khilafat Movement was not the same organisation as the All-India Muslim League.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World II, Class 10, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 54–65 and 68–69; NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 115–124; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, printed pp. 350–358.]

pictures.caption: The Salt Satyagraha connected a national demand with an everyday economic grievance.

title: Khilafat, Non-Cooperation and Mass Politics Across Religious Communities
